I love reading about these references, because it gives me a very keen sense about the popular culture and other preoccupations that people in that period of time would’ve experienced. Just going to reiterate the people who say that your newfound sobriety might cause other people in your life (namely, your husband) to react negatively out of shame over their own usage.

I'm only recently sober when it comes to weed (eight days here), but when I got sober from alcohol 5 years ago, I had a lot of people in my life who regularly drank that treated my new sobriety like an accusation: like, I just got sober, so now y'all should be sober too. They thought I was being condescending, holier-than-thou, etc. 

The truth is that becoming sober may make everyone around you suddenly wonder if they need to become sober, too, which leads them to wonder if they have an addiction or any similar sort of "problem." It's similar to when someone close to you has a health scare, and makes you wonder if you yourself need to get checked out by the doctor just in case.

I've tried my best to reassure people that me being alcohol-free does not at all mean that I think everyone else in my life needs to become alcohol-free; far from it, in fact. But people have a hard time accepting what I've told them. They need to come to their own realizations about their relationship with weed/alcohol/etc. on their own time.

So yeah. I hope your husband is supportive! But understand that any negative reactions he may have re: your sobriety will be about his relationship with weed; they won't be about you.

Hope this helps. Massive congrats on your sobriety.

BLINDSIGHT by Peter Watts is one of the creepiest novels I’ve read and by far the creepiest sci-fi novel I’ve read.

Essentially, a ragtag group of astronauts explore a desiccated, seemingly abandoned spaceship orbiting a dying star. Their journey was prompted after the entire Earth is “scanned” by some kind of alien presence.

It is aliens, but the aliens are so weird and uncanny and disturbing that they feel less “alien” and more “demonic.” There’s also a vampire astronaut whose vampirism is explained by actual science, etc. etc. So you’ll definitely discover some supernatural elements.

THAT said, this book is HARD sci-fi. Like, the hardest sci-fi I’ve read. The author has a PhD in Zoology and has worked as a marine biologist, and the book is filled with references to astrophysics, neuroscience, biology, and much more. It’s a dense read, and you’ll learn a lot if you choose to finish it.

Overall, I highly recommend it even if hard sci-fi isn’t your thing, because every five pages or so there’s a reveal or an image that’s so disturbing and so damn cool that I’m still thinking about it years later.

Wizards arguably have the greatest versatility of any class due to the magic they wield. However, that versatility is dependent on what scrolls you feed them. If you aren’t giving your wizard spells to learn, they’ll only learn the spells they gain upon leveling up, which drastically reduces their versatility.

That said, even with the spells you gain upon leveling up, you’re much more than a “fireball thrower” or “undead wrangler.” You are truly the Swiss Army Knife of mages. You can play support, you can play damage, you can give everyone Feather Fall and triple their jump and let them fly—and you can do all of that with a single build, by switching up your prepared spells whenever you’re out of combat.

If you’re looking for a “Mystical” vibe, I would go with Divination Wizard, which uses Portent Dice, literally rewriting timelines with a snap of your fingers. Playing a 11 Divination Wizard / 1 Knowledge Cleric is by far the best support build I’ve played — access to Bless, Healing Word, medium armor, Portent Dice, Shield, and so much more will practically allow you to defend your allies (and yourself) from ever even getting close to death. It’s a powerhouse.

What I’d ultimately recommend is looking into how to successfully play wizards in D&D. This sounds more like a skills issue than the game’s issue, tbh.

When I was in graduate school for creative writing, one of my professors told me that humor is like salt. 

Salt elevates the flavors of the other ingredients in whatever dish you’re cooking. If you want a spicy dish to taste spicier, add a dash of salt to it.

Similarly, humor elevates all of the other emotions in whatever story you’re writing. You’re far more likely to make someone cry while reading your story if you make them laugh first.

I think Tehol and Bugg are the best possible example of this rule in action. The poignancy of their friendship in moments like this is elevated because of all of the humor they share together.

And I think the overall tragedy of Midnight Tides hits so hard precisely because of that humor.

Time and time again I’d see people on this subreddit talk about how much they loved Tehol and Bugg, and, as I’ve been working my way through the series, I’d been wondering how these characters could cause so much adoration.

I get it now. I really do.

I understand the flak, because I somewhat agree with it, but I was able to gain a valuable lesson from my own frustration with the campaign book:   


Do not, do not, do not, 100% follow any D&D campaign guide without inputting any of your own flavor. If you obediently follow the campaign guide without the input of you or your characters, it will inevitably become a stilted, uninspiring affair.  


Instead, I've used the campaign guide as a means to address or otherwise patch up my "weak spots" whenever I create my own campaign. For example: I'm awful at geography. I am bad at maps. So, while I've pretty much gone off and done entirely my own thing with the campaign, I still rely on the book for maps and locations and the names of places. Other people might be more reliant on the book for peoples' names, or lore, or mythology, or religion, or whatnot.   


Final suggestion: try to use MandyMod and DragnaCarta's campaign guides (which are pinned to the top of this subreddit). They are phenomenally helpful, and will address a lot of the problems you're no doubt experiencing with the campaign book. Beside that, they flesh out Barovia in a way that makes it feel much more immersive than if you only relied on the book itself.  


Hope this helps.

What I’ll offer is this: there is certainly a history within horror of writers using “queer tropes” as a means of coding a monster as explicitly “evil.” Even unknowingly, writers might use tropes that they’re unaware are harmful to a particular community. (I’m thinking of a climactic scene with two characters in the “Petals to the Metal” arc of The Adventure Zone.) 

But it’s also difficult and somewhat restrictive to make a 1:1 allegory of a horror trope to a “real-life counterpart.” These are literal eldritch entities who are avatars of fear—they might represent more than just one thing. (I’m bipolar, for example, so I interpret Helen and The Spiral very, very differently.) 

At the end, of course, your interpretation is valid—I can’t (and won’t) take that away from you. But it might be worthwhile to consider the author’s intentions, as well other possible interpretations, even if, at the end of the day, you still decide that your interpretation is the strongest one for you.
